in_context.text: Paul is describing certain people in Ephesus who had drifted from love, a pure heart, and sincere faith into empty talk. They wanted to be teachers of the law, yet they did not understand their own words or the things they insisted on.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and "own son in the faith," whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The "some" in Ephesus who taught other doctrine, gave heed to fables and endless genealogies, and turned aside to "vain jangling" (empty talk). Timothy was to charge them to stop.

what.text: Paul exposes the would-be teachers. They wanted the role of teaching the law but lacked understanding. They spoke with great confidence about things they did not grasp. Paul then affirms that the law itself is good when it is used rightly.

events.text: This happened after Paul urged Timothy to stay in Ephesus while Paul went on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, by Paul, between his Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and see it as written in Paul's name by a follower; others defend Paul's authorship and the earlier date.

where.text: Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia, where Timothy was leading the church. The letter does not say where Paul wrote it from, though he had gone to Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul explains what is wrong with the false teachers so Timothy can confront them. Their teaching produced questions and arguments rather than the godly building up that comes by faith.

big_picture.text: The aim of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. The problem was not the law, which is good if used lawfully, but teachers who misused it without understanding. This fits the letter's theme that sound teaching and godly living belong together.

for_readers.text: Wanting to teach and speaking confidently do not make someone a sound teacher. Elsewhere Scripture warns against the same pattern: those who teach others but not themselves, and those proud yet "knowing nothing."

why_it_matters.text: This rare word is used elsewhere in the New Testament for recognized teachers of the Jewish law. It shows these people wanted a formal, respected teaching role, not just a casual say.
The word means to affirm confidently or insist. The point is not that they were unsure, but that they were very sure about things they did not understand.
This verb means to perceive with the mind. Their failure was a lack of real understanding, both of their own words and of their subject.

takeaway.text: Paul warns that a desire to teach, joined with confident talk, is dangerous without real understanding. Good teaching aims at love, a pure heart, and sincere faith.

unsupported.reason: The lexicon entry only lists Luke 5:17 and Acts 5:34 as other uses. It does not say these refer to recognized or respected Jewish law teachers. It also does not show that the people in 1 Timothy wanted a formal, respected teaching role; that inference goes beyond the cited source.
